speaker: Horace He
title: Horace He: Building Machine Learning Systems for a Trillion Trillion Floating Point Operations
question: In deep learning training, why can recomputing intermediate activations from scratch actually make a model run faster?
guest: Even when all your data already lives in GPU VRAM, VRAM is not where the compute units are located. To run any operation, you have to move data from VRAM to on-chip SRAM near the compute units and back—like hauling supplies between a distant warehouse and a small factory. That data movement is the memory bandwidth cost, and it accounts for a huge share of GPU runtime. Because moving tensors back and forth is so expensive, you often face a recomputation versus reuse trade-off. By recomputing a value from data already sitting on-chip instead of storing it to global memory and reloading it later, you significantly reduce memory accesses. That way, recomputation not only cuts peak memory usage, it can also improve actual runtime performance. This trade-off is uniquely important in machine learning because program lifetimes look very unusual compared to typical software. Normally, intermediates are short-lived and quickly discarded. In machine learning, you run the forward pass from layer zero through the last layer, then run backpropagation in reverse, forcing you to keep intermediate activations alive across the entire pass.

points.core: Shuttling tensors from GPU global memory to on-chip compute units dominates runtime.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Recomputing activations can be faster because modern training is usually limited by memory and memory traffic, not by raw arithmetic.

Backpropagation normally stores every intermediate activation from the forward pass so the backward pass can reuse them. Those stored tensors dominate GPU memory. Writing them out and reading them back costs memory bandwidth, and many operations (such as normalisation, activations or attention scores) are cheap to compute relative to the cost of moving their large outputs through memory. Recomputing such a value from inputs already in cache or on-chip can take less time than fetching a saved copy, which is why fused kernels and compilers that "rematerialise" cheap intermediates often speed things up.

The bigger effect is indirect. Dropping stored activations (gradient checkpointing, reversible layers) frees memory, which lets you use larger batches, improving GPU utilisation and throughput. It also avoids slow fallbacks such as out-of-memory retries, swapping to host memory, allocator fragmentation, or splitting the model across devices.

So although recomputation adds floating-point work (typically about one extra forward pass for checkpointing), that work is cheap compared with the memory bottleneck it removes. Where memory isn't the constraint, recomputation is simply slower.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Modern GPUs have vastly outpaced memory bandwidth in raw compute speed, making many deep learning operations memory-bound rather than compute-bound. During standard training, intermediate activations—such as large attention matrices or pointwise layer outputs—must be written from fast on-chip SRAM to much slower off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in the forward pass, then fetched back into SRAM during backpropagation. When activations take less time to calculate than to transfer, recomputing them from cached inputs on the fly inside SRAM is faster than waiting on HBM round-trips. IO-aware algorithms like FlashAttention and compiler operator fusion exploit this hardware asymmetry, trading abundant FLOPs for scarce memory bandwidth while cutting kernel launch overhead.

Recomputation can also boost end-to-end training speed at the system level by drastically shrinking peak activation memory. The freed HBM allows models to run with larger micro-batches—increasing arithmetic intensity and GPU utilization—or eliminates the need for CPU offloading and extra cross-device parallelism over even slower interconnects.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Recomputing activations can make training faster because on modern GPUs and TPUs, arithmetic is cheap and moving data is expensive. Accelerators can do far more FLOPs per second than they can move bytes to and from high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Many operations, such as attention softmax, layer norms, activation functions and dropout, are limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute.

Storing a large intermediate means writing it to HBM in the forward pass and reading it back in the backward pass. That round trip can take longer than recomputing the values on-chip from smaller inputs that are already available. FlashAttention is the standard example. It never stores the N×N attention matrix. Instead, it recomputes the attention matrix tile by tile in fast SRAM during the backward pass. This adds FLOPs but cuts HBM traffic sharply, so it runs faster as well as using less memory.

There is also an indirect gain. Freeing activation memory lets you use larger micro-batches, which improves hardware utilization. It can also let you avoid slower workarounds such as offloading to CPU, heavier model or pipeline parallelism, or extra gradient-accumulation steps. Selective checkpointing, which recomputes only the cheap, memory-heavy operations, is designed to get these benefits at minimal compute cost.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: On modern GPUs, training is often bottlenecked by memory bandwidth and memory capacity rather than raw arithmetic throughput. Recomputing intermediate activations during the backward pass—known as activation checkpointing or rematerialization—can speed up training in two main ways. First, reading and writing large intermediate tensors to off-chip high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is much slower than performing math inside fast on-chip SRAM and registers. For memory-bound operations, such as elementwise layers or the attention matrix in FlashAttention, discarding intermediates and recalculating them on-chip eliminates expensive HBM traffic, making the step faster despite doing more floating-point operations. Second, freeing up GPU memory allows training with larger batch sizes or less cross-device communication and CPU offloading. Larger batches keep the GPU's compute units saturated and amortize overhead across more examples, often increasing overall training throughput enough to more than offset the extra recomputation work.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Recomputing activations can be faster because moving data can cost more time than doing the arithmetic again. During training, the forward pass can save intermediate activations to GPU memory for the backward pass. That means writing them out and reading them back later. If an activation is cheap to reconstruct from values already on the chip, recomputing it during backpropagation can avoid both trips to GPU memory.

FlashAttention is a concrete example. It reconstructs blocks of attention probabilities during the backward pass, avoiding the need to store and reload the full attention matrix. The GPU does more arithmetic, but it can finish sooner because it spends less time waiting for data. The speedup depends on whether the memory traffic saved outweighs the extra computation.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
During training, backpropagation needs intermediate activations from the forward pass. Saving every activation can mean writing large tensors to GPU memory and reading them back later. When memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, the GPU can repeat a few cheap calculations faster than it can fetch their results. Recomputing those activations close to where they’re used can therefore shorten a training step, even though it increases the number of operations.

Recomputation also reduces peak memory use. That can improve training throughput by allowing a larger batch that uses the GPU more fully, or by avoiding transfers to and from CPU memory. If computation is already the bottleneck and the batch size stays fixed, recomputation usually slows training.
